blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a comprehensive study revealing the pervasive nature of third-party tracking in the Android app ecosystem through Advertising and Tracking Services (ATS). The paper exposes how a small number of dominant companies (notably Alphabet and Facebook) control a disproportionate share of tracking data, often without transparency or user consent. The study leverages the Lumen Privacy Monitor app to analyze network traffic from 11,000 users, uncovering that 82% of apps connect to at least one ATS domain, with many leaking unique identifiers like Android IDs and IMEIs. The authors also demonstrate cross-device tracking potential and highlight regulatory gaps, showing how user data flows across borders to jurisdictions with weaker privacy protections. The findings underscore the need for stronger enforcement of privacy laws like GDPR.
paper_title: Apps, trackers, privacy, and regulators: a global study of the mobile tracking ecosystem
paper_abstract: We investigate the privacy compliance processes followed by developers of child-directed mobile apps. While children’s online privacy laws have existed for decades in the US, prior research found relatively low rates of compliance. Yet, little is known about how compliance issues come to exist and how compliance processes can be improved to address them. Our results, based on surveys (n = 127) and interviews (n = 27), suggest that most developers rely on app markets to identify privacy issues, they lack complete understandings of the third-party SDKs they integrate, and they find it challenging to ensure that these SDKs are kept upto-date and privacy-related options are configured correctly. As a result, we find that well-resourced app developers outsource most compliance decisions to auditing services, and that smaller developers follow “best-effort” models, by assuming that their apps are compliant so long as they have not been rejected by app markets. We highlight the need for usable tools that help developers identify and fix mobile app privacy issues. Keywords: Privacy compliance, Software developers, Children privacy, Google Play, SDKs DOI 10.56553/popets-2022-0108 Received 2022-02-28; revised 2022-06-15; accepted 2022-06-16.
